about: Burdigala (Bordeaux, the old Roman city on the Garonne), written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/burdigala.md and the spine. One port. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what the sources do not show. The dossier's section 8 lists what must not be claimed, and this file keeps to it: the bishop and count of 793 are not known, no quay, toll, market day, moneyer or merchant is recorded, no text of these years names wine shipped from here, the betrayal of 848 is one distant bishop's line and is never told as fact, and whether Northmen ruled the town after 848 is left open.
woven: Woven with Quentovic, Rotomagus, Parisius, Namnetis and Herio on 6 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways, burdigala.oil_seller made real (Felix, whom the Herio cellarer's tie and story named), beats placed across the region and the port's cards (encounters/neustria_west_793.json) put on their sites. Nothing was taken out.

ports.summary: An old Roman city of Aquitaine, four-square behind a wall of grey stone on the left bank of the Garonne, with marsh on three sides and a hundred kilometres of brown tidal water between it and the sea. In 793 it belongs to the kingdom King Charles made for his son Louis; the Gascons live across the river. A merchant comes for the wine of the country, cheap after the vintage, and for a little salt and dried fish from the river mouth, and he comes with a pilot or not at all.
ports.seasons: The year turns on the vintage: grapes are cut from Holy Cross day in September into October, and new wine is cheapest from then to Christmas and dearest before the next harvest. The tide rules every day of it: the flood carries a boat up from the sea and the ebb takes her down, and at the spring tides of late summer, when the river is low, a wave runs up the Garonne ahead of the flood (?). Saint Amand is kept on 18 June and Saint Seurin in October (the day here is not checked (?)); the sea shuts at Martinmas.

history.text: King Charles sets a count named Seguin over Bordeaux when he orders Aquitaine. Whether the same man still holds it in 793 is not recorded.
history.source: The Astronomer, Vita Hludowici ch. 3 (la.wikisource.org/wiki/Vita_Ludovici); dossier 1

history.text: Louis, the young king of Aquitaine, is away in Italy in the spring. The list of the city's bishops is blank from the seventh century to Sicharius.
Bordeaux is one of the twenty-one chief cities named in the emperor's will, each to have its share of his treasure.

Louis the Pious gives the bishop's church of Saint Andrew its immunity, with Saint Mary's church and Saint Helen's chapel beside it. Sicharius is the first bishop named in two hundred years. Pennies are struck with BVRDIGALA in two lines.
history.source: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathédrale_Saint-André_de_Bordeaux; Gallia Christiana II (1720) cols 796-803; Prou, Les monnaies carolingiennes (1896); dossier 2, 3

history.text: Seguin, called duke of the Gascons, is put out of his office for arrogance and wicked ways, and the Gascons beyond the river rise.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 816, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seguin_I_of_Gascony; dossier 5

history.text: This year the Northmen went up the Garonne as far as Toulouse, plundering on every side, and nobody stood against them.
In the autumn the Northmen broke out between Bordeaux and Saintes. The Christians fought them on foot and were cut down; Count Seguin was taken and killed, and Saintes burned.
history.source: Lupus of Ferrières, letter 31 (Migne's number); Chronicon Aquitanicum 845, MGH SS II p. 253; dossier 5

history.text: This year the Danes lay about Bordeaux and besieged it for a long time.

In Lent King Charles took nine Danish ships on the Dordogne. After that the Northmen took Bordeaux by night, with William its duke, and wasted and burned it. One annal, written far off, says the Jews betrayed it; others read that as Pippin's party. The Aquitanians, sick of Pippin's sloth, chose Charles at Orléans. Melle, the silver mint to the north, was sacked the same year.
history.source: Chronicon Fontanellense 848 and Chronicon Aquitanicum 848, MGH SS II pp. 253, 302-303; Annales Bertiniani 848; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepin_II_of_Aquitaine; dossier 5, 8

history.text: On 13 October the fleet of Asgeir, come from Bordeaux, a place most strongly fortified, entered the Seine. The next June it went back to Bordeaux laden.
history.source: Chronicon Fontanellense 851, MGH SS II pp. 302-303; dossier 5

history.text: The Northmen are at Bordeaux again, roaming as they please. They winter in the country in 848, 855 and 864.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 855; Boutoulle 2008, Par peur des Normands (abstract, hal.science/hal-00847367v1); dossier 5

history.text: At Ponthion Archbishop Frotar pleads that he could not stay in his city for the pagans. The pope lets him have Bourges for as long as the pagans hold the church of Bordeaux.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 876; Gallia Christiana II cols 796-803; dossier 5

history.text: Amalvinus, count of Bordeaux, is at the council of Bourges.

A letter in the name of Alfonso, king in Spain, says he will buy a crown of gold and gems from the clergy of Tours; it is to wait at Bordeaux with 'our friend' Amalvinus for his ships in May. Some scholars doubt the letter.

Before this year Count William the Good, son of Raymond and Entregodis, rebuilds Holy Cross in the marsh for thirteen monks under Abbot Elis, on the counsel of young Trencard, and gives it lands with vines and the oratory of Saint Mary at Soulac with its pine wood and fishery.
history.source: Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 2 (la.wikisource.org/wiki/Gallia_Christiana_1720_02/Instrumenta/Burdigalensis); dossier 2, 7

history.text: On 1 June Gombaud, archbishop of Bordeaux, presides at Charroux, where the bishops curse any who break into churches, strike unarmed clergy or take a poor man's beasts.

Geoffrey, a Frank by birth and honest in his ways, is chosen archbishop and anointed at Blaye before Duke Sancho's assembly. A charter of the same date gives Holy Cross the road toll of Saint-Macaire and a custom of three measures of salt.
history.source: Gallia Christiana II cols 796-803 and Instrumenta no. 4 (its Latin was suspect by the 13th century); dossier 3, 4

history.text: On 10 March Eudes of Poitou, who held Bordeaux and Gascony, is killed. Bernard of Armagnac disputes the county until Guy Geoffrey wins it, in 1044 or 1052.
history.source: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eudes_de_Poitiers; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comté_de_Bordeaux; Poey d'Avant, Monnaies féodales II (1860); dossier 5

eras.text: A quiet walled city of King Louis's Aquitaine: half its Roman ground is garden and ruin, the old harbour inside the wall is mud, and boats lie on the river bank. The bishop's chair has no name on it in the lists. Country wine is the trade, and the Gascons across the water are the worry.

Seguin is put out and the Gascons rise, but the city is busier than it has been: a bishop again, the king's pennies struck with the city's name, Pippin's court passing through (?). Wine goes down the river and good silver comes up from Melle.

The Northmen are on the Garonne. In 844 they pass upriver to Toulouse; in 845 the count is killed on the Saintes road; in 847 they sit round the wall for a long time. Wine lies unsold in every cellar and a boat that can get out to sea names her own price. In 848 the city is taken by night and burned.

The pagans' years. Fleets come and go from the river and winter in the country; the archbishop cannot stay in his city and lives at Bourges. Whether the Northmen hold the town or only use it nobody far away can say (the sources dispute it). No mint, little law, and trade only for those who can deal with both sides.

A count sits here again and the wall is patched with stone from the Arenas; armed men on horses are a thing the town now has. Ships from Spain are spoken of. The churches outside the wall are roofless or poor, and the pennies are thin.

The dukes of the Gascons hold the city and it mends: Holy Cross rebuilt in the marsh, canons at Saint Seurin, an archbishop who leads the bishops at Charroux. The duke's pennies say SANCHIVS and want weighing.

Poitou's counts and then Guy Geoffrey hold Bordeaux, and in the years between nobody quite does. Stone churches go up at Saint Seurin and Saint Andrew. Pilgrims for Spain cross here in growing numbers (?), and the wine of the abbeys' vines is worth a ship's coming.

sites.name: The bank under the wall
sites.see: A long bend of brown river, wide as a lake, and a bank of grey mud and gravel under a high stone wall with round towers. Boats sit canted on the mud at low water: flat river barges, small fishing boats, now and then a sea-going hull. Planks are laid from the gravel to the firm ground. Behind the wall, to the north, a row of tall white columns stands against the sky. Gulls, the slap of the tide turning, the smell of mud and pitch.
sites.source: The Roman basin inside the wall silted from the 6th century and work moved to the river bank; the river about 700 m wide at the crescent bend; no quay of these years is known, so this is a bank and the table's 'quay' is unproven (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_de_Bordeaux; dossier 1). The planks are assumed (?).

sites.name: The water gate and Saint Peter's
sites.see: A dark arch in the wall where a stream runs out across the mud, with a small old church of patched stone hard beside it, its door open to the river. Through the arch a reedy hollow shows where ships once lay inside the city. A man with a tally stick sits on a block by the gate; women wash at the stream. A cracked bell, wet stone, candle smoke.
sites.source: Porta Navigera, the water gate by Saint Peter's, at the old harbour mouth; Saint Peter's is the harbour church in Gregory of Tours and is then unnamed until 1173 (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remparts_et_portes_de_ville_de_Bordeaux; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Église_Saint-Pierre_de_Bordeaux; dossier 2). No toll is recorded for Bordeaux: the man at the gate is the game's (?).

sites.name: The wine sellers by the old harbour
sites.see: An open space of trodden earth inside the water gate, on the rim of the silted basin, with Roman paving showing through in places. Casks lie on their sides under lean-to roofs against old walls; a woman tips a dipper for a buyer to taste; sacks of grey salt and strings of dried fish hang at one end. Vine smoke, sour must, flies, the knock of a mallet on a hoop.
sites.source: No market, market day or fair is recorded for Bordeaux in these years (dossier 4): the place is assumed (?). Goods agree with goods_793.json (aquitaine_wine made in aquitaine; sea_salt a little); salt and the fishery from Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta nos 2 and 4.

sites.name: Saint Andrew's, the bishop's church
sites.see: A long low church of small Roman stones and reused marble against the inside of the west wall, with a smaller church and a chapel close by it and a yard between where clerks walk. Inside it is dim, with one lamp before the altar and a cupboard of books chained shut. Singing at the hours; cold stone; wax.
sites.source: Saint Andrew's by the west wall, with Saint Mary's and Saint Helen's chapel in the immunity of 814; said to be wrecked in 848 and 864; rebuilt in the 11th century (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathédrale_Saint-André_de_Bordeaux; dossier 2). The book cupboard is assumed (?).

sites.name: The count's enclosure
sites.see: A walled yard inside the city with a gate you must knock at: a long hall with a tiled roof in poor repair, a chapel, a well with a stone rim, horses tied under a fig tree. Men with spears sit in the shade and stand when the count's steward crosses. Dogs, horse dung, a smith's hammer somewhere behind.
sites.source: The enclosure at Saint-Projet with a hall ('la Salle'), a chapel, the mint, gates and a well is known only from 11th- to 13th-century texts and the street plan and has never been dug: its date is open, and it is placed here in 793 as an assumption (?) (Boutoulle and Jean-Courret 2016, abstract, hal.science/hal-01453148v1; dossier 2). Not the Ombrière, whose tower is first named in 1080.

sites.name: The moneyer's bench
sites.see: A low room off the count's yard with a barred window: a block of oak with an iron die set in it, a second die in a man's fist, a hammer, a pan of blank silver discs and a scale hung from a beam. Each blow rings like a small bell. Charcoal, hot metal, a boy sweeping the floor for clippings.
sites.source: No penny of Charles from Bordeaux in Prou; Louis the Pious BVRDIGALA in two lines; Lothar I BVRDICALA round a temple, 1.60 g; King Lothar (954-986) 'Burdegal'; then the counts' poor silver SANCHIVS (0.76 to 1.30 g), BERNARDV, GVILELMO (Prou 1896; Poey d'Avant 1860; dossier 2). The mint lay in the Saint-Projet enclosure in later texts. No striking is assumed between 848 and 887 (?).

sites.name: The pillars
sites.see: Just outside the north wall, on the highest ground, two dozen white columns as tall as five houses stand in a square with no roof, carved figures along the top and sky between them. Goats graze inside. From the river they are the first thing seen of the city and the last thing lost. Wind in dry grass, jackdaws, warm stone.
sites.source: The columns of a roofless Roman temple, 26 m high, 'seen from afar', 24 when whole and 17 still standing in 1669 (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piliers_de_Tutelle; dossier 1). Nobody worships here: the old gods are only ruins and a gate's name (dossier 6). The kind 'shrine' is the nearest in the brief's list.

sites.name: The Arenas
sites.see: North-west of the wall a great oval of broken arches stands in the vines, taller than the city wall and open to the sky. Men with bars and wedges are prising squared blocks out of its lower tiers and sledging them away behind oxen. Brambles in the arena floor. Stone dust, the creak of a sledge, lizards on the warm blocks.
sites.source: The ruined amphitheatre, 132 by 111 m, used as a stone quarry and called 'the Arenas' in the 10th century; not 'Palais Gallien', a name of 1367 (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Gallien; dossier 1, 8).

sites.name: Saint Seurin's among the graves
sites.see: Outside the west gate, the gate of Jove, a road runs through a field of the dead: stone coffins lying lid to lid in rows, some stacked, grass between them, and in the middle a low old church over the saint's tomb with its door worn hollow. Old women sell candles at the wall. Larks, a spade working, incense when the door opens.
sites.source: A burial church over Saint Seurin's tomb, first built about 450, in a grave field used from the 4th to the 13th century: 435 burials dug, 265 in stone coffins up to five deep, 70 in amphorae; canons about 990; rebuilt early in the 11th century (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilique_Saint-Seurin_de_Bordeaux; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nécropole_Saint-Seurin_de_Bordeaux; Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 3; dossier 2, 6). Porta Jovia is the west gate. The candle sellers and healing at the tomb are assumed (?).

sites.name: Holy Cross in the marsh
sites.see: South of the wall a causeway of logs crosses reed and black water to a rise of dry ground beside a stream. In 793 there is an old oratory there with a sagging roof and one keeper; after the pagans, bare walls; from the 970s a new stone church, a cloister of thirteen monks, vines on the slope and a press-house. Frogs, a mill wheel on the stream, new mortar.
sites.source: Holy Cross south of the wall by the Eau Bourde: a Merovingian house where Mommolin, abbot of Fleury, died about 679; 'destroyed by the pagans'; rebuilt before 977 by Count William the Good for thirteen monks and Abbot Elis, with 'lands with vines' (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbatiale_Sainte-Croix_de_Bordeaux; Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 2; dossier 2). What stood there in 793 is not known: the oratory with one keeper follows the old men's memory in the charter (?).

sites.name: The house by the Broken Tower
sites.see: A long room built against the inside of the city wall where a tower has lost its top, the Roman stone for a back wall and a vine over the door. Benches, a cask on trestles, a hearth in the middle of the floor with the smoke going out through the thatch. River men at one end, Gascons with their own knives at the other. Sour wine, onions, wet wool.
sites.source: Invented. A 'Broken Tower' stood by a mill given to Saint Seurin between 1027 and 1043 (Gallia Christiana II; dossier 3): the name is borrowed for 793 (?). Thin country wine is poured here beside ale because this is vine country: an assumption (?), since the brief keeps wine for lords and the Mass elsewhere.

sites.name: The boat bank below the stream
sites.see: Downstream of the wall, where a second stream comes out through reeds, a slope of gravel with two hulls on it: a flat barge with new pale planks let into her side and a small boat upside down for pitching. Oak logs from upriver lie half floated at the water's edge. An adze, a pitch pot bubbling, smoke blown flat along the bank.
sites.source: Invented: no yard or shipman is recorded (dossier 3). The streams are the Devèze and the Peugue, at whose mouths the city lies (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burdigala; dossier 1). Oak rafted down the Garonne is assumed (?).

people.name: Seguin
people.trait: A hard border lord who has held one river against one people for fifteen years and thinks that is the whole of the world.
people.want: Horses, mail and news of the king, in that order; and to be left alone to deal with the Gascons his own way.
people.fear: A king's man riding in with a letter and a list of what has been said about him.
people.voice: Short and loud, in Frankish. Speaks the country's Romance badly on purpose. Asks what a thing costs before he asks what it is.
people.looks: About forty-five in 793, thick in the neck, cropped grey-brown hair, a long moustache and a shaved chin, a red tunic to the knee, a sword on a baldric and a hawking glove in his belt.
knows: who may trade across the river with the Gascons and who may not
where King Louis is this season
what a horse or a mail coat fetches south of the Loire
which roads north are safe: by Saintes to Poitiers

ties.note: her house was great here before any Frank; she will not rise when he comes in
the pilot brought his wine boats through the banks for years on a promise
the count on the Breton march gets the king's praise; the count on the Gascon one gets letters
the abbot of Saint Martin's writes about his house's wine and its passage; Seguin has not answered (?)

lines.greet: A boat from the north. Good. What do you carry, what does it cost, and who told you this river was open to you?
lines.greet_again: The northern boatman. You came back through the banks, so you can be taught. Sit. Not there.
rumour: The king is over the mountains with his brother this year. When the king is away every Gascon grows a hand taller.
They want me to sit in a court and hear two farmers out. I was given this city to hold, not to listen to.
Bring me mail and I will not ask where it was made. Carry mail across that river and I will hang you.
lines.saying: A river is a wall that moves. Watch it twice as hard.
lines.to_heir: Your father stood where you stand and asked for less. I remember him as a man who paid.
lines.farewell: Go down on the ebb. If the Gascons hail you from the far bank, you did not hear them.

people.source: Real: the count set over Bordeaux in 778 (the Astronomer, ch. 3), probably the 'duke of the Gascons' deposed in 816 for arrogance and wicked ways (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seguin_I_of_Gascony; dossier 3). That he holds the city in 793 is not recorded (?). His birth year, looks and manner are invented; Louis's journey to Italy in 793 is chronicle_793.json.

people.name: Amantius
people.trait: Knows the river mouth the way a man knows his own stair in the dark, and is patient with those who do not.
people.want: His grandson to learn the banks before his own eyes go, and a fair fee paid in silver, not in promises.
people.fear: The year the sand moves in winter and he takes a stranger's ship onto it in front of everyone.
people.voice: Slow, in the Romance of the town, with river words nobody north has. Counts tides on his fingers. Never says a thing is safe, only that it was yesterday.
people.looks: About forty-five in 793, lean and stooped, brown as a nut, white stubble, a short sleeveless cloak of goat hair, bare feet, a sounding pole taller than himself marked with rings of red cord.
knows: where the channel lies through the banks of the river mouth this year
the hour of the flood at the town and at Blaye
when the wave comes up the river ahead of the tide
which skippers are in the river and who went out and did not come back
what salt fetches at the river mouth

ties.note: drinks at her house and brings her the river's news first
pilots the count's boats and is owed for three seasons
the island's pilot hands him the salt boats at the river mouth and takes his news back north (?)
each says the other's river is a ditch with a tide in it
they have never met; skippers carry each one's greeting and each one's opinion of the other's river
tells the oil seller which hulls ride steady enough for jars, and is paid in a spoonful for his bread

lines.greet: You came up without a pilot. Then God likes you, or the tide was high. Next time take me from Blaye and keep your keel.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat. Good. The north bank moved since Easter; I will show you with the pole, not with words.
rumour: The river is eight of your miles wide at the mouth and a man's height deep in most of it. Wide is not the same as open.
At the big tides after harvest a wave walks up ahead of the flood. Lie in midstream and face it. Boats on the mud are rolled.
A boat with salt from the island went aground off the point on Tuesday. They floated her on the next flood, lighter by a third.
lines.saying: The sea lends the river to us twice a day and takes it back.
lines.to_heir: Your father paid me at the gate, before he sold. I told my grandson: that is how you know a man.
lines.farewell: Leave at the top of the tide and not after. Keep the pillars over your stern as long as you can see them.

people.source: Invented; no shipman or pilot is named for Bordeaux (dossier 3). Amantius is a saint's name of the city (Saint Amand, 18 June), as Aquitanians bore Roman and saints' names (Design/content/peoples/frankish.md). The estuary, its banks, width and bore: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gironde_(estuaire); Blaye on the right bank: Gallia Christiana II. His miles are Roman miles: the estuary is up to 12 km wide, which is about eight of them.

people.name: Placidina
people.trait: The last of a house that says it had senators in it: sells its wine by the cup with a straight back and forgets no slight in two hundred years.
people.want: The house's vines kept, the house's one old book read by somebody who deserves it, and the Franks to learn some manners.
people.fear: Dying with the cellar full, the book unread and the roof sold to a Frank for stabling.
people.voice: Exact and a little grand, in good Romance with Latin words where they fit. Corrects people. Is kind to the hungry and does not let it be mentioned.
people.looks: About fifty in 793, small and upright, white hair under a dark veil, a long plain gown of good old cloth mended at the cuffs, a ring with a carved red stone, a bunch of iron keys.
knows: what the new wine will fetch and whose is watered
who slept in the city last night and why
which of the clerks at Saint Andrew's can copy and which only says so
the old names of the gates and the ruins
what the poet of the city wrote about it, by heart

ties.note: he has drunk on her bench for thirty years and still pays
she calls him 'the Frank' to his steward and 'lord count' to his face, with the same look
the abbot at Tours has heard there is an old book of verses here and has written to ask for a copy (?)
the Northumbrian letter-carrier came once on foot from the Loire, read half the book standing and wept at leaving it (?)
two widows who send each other salt and wine by the same boats and have never met (?)
the English monk at the Loire sent to ask about her book, in careful Latin (?)
her house bought oil of his father; she pays on the day and tells him what it used to cost

lines.greet: You are from the north, and not a Frank. Good. Sit. This is my own wine: thin, honest, and a penny for three cups.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who washes his hands. I kept your bench. Tell me what they say at the Loire before you drink.
rumour: The new wine is good on the gravel and poor by the marsh this year. Buy from the gravel, and taste from the middle of the cask.
There has been no bishop here that anyone can name since my grandmother's grandmother. The clerks keep the feasts, and sell the candle ends.
This city had a school when Rome did. Now a count asks me what a book is for.
lines.saying: Never call an Aquitanian a Frank. He will forgive you, and remember.
lines.to_heir: You have your father's way of standing in a door. He listened when I read to him. Do you listen?
lines.farewell: Go with God and the ebb. Bring me back a clerk who can read, or failing that, pepper.

people.source: Invented. Placidina is an attested name of the city: the wife of Bishop Leontius II in the 6th century bore it (Venantius Fortunatus (?)); this ordinary widow shares only the name. The old senatorial houses, Roman law and Aquitanian pride: Design/content/peoples/frankish.md. The blank in the bishops' list: dossier 1. The book is Ausonius's (see the story burdigala.poets_book).

people.name: Bertric
people.trait: A careful, cheerful man who trusts his scale and nothing else, and says so to counts.
people.want: Clean silver from Melle, a die that does not crack, and nobody leaning on his bench while he works.
people.fear: A light penny with his city's name on it, found in the king's own chest.
people.voice: Quick and plain, in Frankish and Romance mixed. Talks while he strikes, in time with the hammer. Weighs your coin while you are still greeting him.
people.looks: About thirty in 820, short and broad in the shoulder, a singed leather apron, a round felt cap, burn scars on both hands, a small hand balance on a cord round his neck.
knows: what a penny of this mint weighs and what the old ones are worth melted
what silver costs at Melle this year
whose pennies are light: he keeps a board of bad ones nailed up
what the king has ordered about coin

ties.note: the merchant brings him foreign silver to try and they argue about weights for pleasure
learned die-cutting from a man who learned it at Dorestad under the old moneyer (?)
says the Seine mint's pennies come out a grain short and keeps three on his board to prove it (?)

lines.greet: Put it on the pan before you tell me what it is. Good. Now tell me, and we will see who is right.
lines.greet_again: The northern purse. Last time you had two pennies I would not have struck. Let us see what you have learned.
rumour: Melle sends me less silver each year and more excuses. The hill is not empty; the carters are afraid of the road.
The new king wants his own name on the die by Easter. Kings change faster than dies wear out, these days.
A Gascon tried to pay his fine in tin washed with silver. I nailed it up there. He comes to look at it.
lines.saying: A penny has two faces and one weight. Believe the weight.
lines.to_heir: Your father let me weigh him without sulking. Put your purse there, and do not watch my hands, watch the beam.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If they offer you my pennies in the north at a discount, buy them, and tell me who was selling.

people.source: Invented; no moneyer is named for Bordeaux (dossier 3). Bert- and -ric are Frankish name parts (Design/content/peoples/frankish.md). The coins of Louis the Pious and Lothar I: Prou 1896; Melle as Aquitaine's silver, sacked in 848: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siège_de_Bordeaux_(847); his death in the year the city fell is the game's.

people.name: Natan
people.trait: A dealer in wine, salt and whatever comes from Spain, who keeps his word because he cannot afford not to, and his temper for the same reason.
people.want: His household and his people's scrolls out of the city before the river brings the ships again, and somewhere to take them.
people.fear: Being blamed. He has read enough to know who is blamed when a wall fails.
people.voice: Even and careful, in the town's Romance. Answers a question with a better question. Dry when he is afraid.
people.looks: About forty in 840, tall and narrow, a trimmed black beard going grey, a long dark gown belted with a plain cord, a wax tablet at his belt, ink on his right thumb.
knows: what wine and salt fetch here and at the Loire
what comes over the mountains from Spain and when
who in the city owes and who pays
which of the tellings about the Northmen are true, as far as a man can know

ties.note: they try each other's weights and have never found a fault, to the grief of both
buys the island abbey's salt on a year's credit and has always paid at Martinmas (?)
the salter who stayed on the island sells to him still, and asks no questions about the buyers
after the fire the Seine merchant buys from Natan's sons at the Loire (?)
the Frisian's grandsons buy wine here in good years and undercut him at the Loire

lines.greet: You have a boat that can cross the bar. Then we should talk now, and about more than wine.
lines.greet_again: You came back up a river other men are leaving. Either you are brave, or you know a price I do not.
rumour: The ships went up to Toulouse and nobody stood against them. A river that carries wine down carries anything up.
The count is dead on the Saintes road. Men swear to it. When men swear to news, it is bad and it is true.
Wine is cheaper inside this wall than water is outside it. I would sell you my cellar for the price of a passage.
lines.saying: When the wall holds they thank the saint. When it falls they look for a stranger.
lines.to_heir: Your father carried what I asked and said nothing in the ale-houses. I have told my sons your name.
lines.farewell: Go down by night on the ebb and show no light. If anyone asks who sent you, you bought from the market.

people.source: Invented. Jews are named at Bordeaux once, in 848 (Annales Bertiniani); no merchant of any people is named (dossier 3). The annal's charge of betrayal is one line by a distant bishop, and some read it as Pippin's party: it is never stated as fact (dossier 8; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepin_II_of_Aquitaine). 'people' is set to romance because the peoples table has no row for him: see the report's needs.

people.name: Amalvinus
people.trait: A count of a half-ruined city who has learned to be everybody's friend and to keep a fast horse.
people.want: Ships in his river that are not Northmen's, and a name that reaches as far as Spain and Tours.
people.fear: Sails at the river mouth in a number nobody has counted to before.
people.voice: Courteous and slow, in Romance. Calls every stranger 'friend' and watches his hands. Writes nothing down himself.
people.looks: About forty in 890, tall and spare, fair hair gone thin, a short blue cloak pinned at the right shoulder, a sword with a silver-wired hilt, a letter folded small in his fist.
knows: which stretches of the wall are sound
when the ships from Spain are looked for: in May
what the bishops said at Bourges
who holds the Loire mouth this year

ties.note: sends word north to the count on the Seine whenever sails leave his river (?)
the fleets that winter on the Seine have wintered on the Garonne
has never seen him; every count on a western river has the same enemy on the Seine

lines.greet: Welcome, friend. A merchant in my river is the best news since Easter. Whose man are you, and whose are you not?
lines.greet_again: My friend from the north. The wall is higher than when you left, and the wine is the same. Come in.
rumour: The stone for the wall comes from the Arenas. The old people built a place for games; we take it apart to stay alive.
There is a king in Spain who calls me friend in a letter. I am waiting for his ships. They come in May, if they come.
My archbishop's grandfather in office lived at Bourges and never saw his own church. I intend to die in this city.
lines.saying: A count without ships has a river. A count with ships has a road.
lines.to_heir: Your people have come up this river since before the fire. That is older than my county. Sit by me.
lines.farewell: Go well, friend. Tell them at the Loire that Bordeaux has a count, a wall and wine, in that order.

people.source: Real: Count Amalvinus of Bordeaux, at the council of Bourges in 887 and named in the letter of 906 as 'our friend' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalvinus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistola_Adefonsi_Hispaniae_regis; dossier 3, 7). The wall strengthened in the late 9th century, when armed men first appear: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histoire_de_Bordeaux. His birth year, looks and manner are invented; Frotar's exile is Annales Bertiniani 876.

people.name: Trencard
people.trait: A young noble who can read, which makes him either the cleverest man in the hall or the oddest, depending on the hour.
people.want: The monks back on his family's ground at the Holy Cross, and his name in their book when he is dead.
people.fear: That he gave away his grandfather's land for a thing that will burn again.
people.voice: Quick and earnest, in Romance, with Latin when he forgets himself. Quotes old men. Laughs at his own learning before others can.
people.looks: About twenty-five in 975, slight, dark hair cut straight across the brow, a green tunic with a woven border, a short sword he wears badly, a small book in a leather bag at his hip.
knows: what the old men remember of the monks in the marsh
what the count means to give Holy Cross: vines, Soulac, the fishery
which of the count's household can be trusted with a tally
what is written in the charters, word for word

ties.note: as an old man he tells the new archbishop where every charter lies and what it left out (?)
in his old age the Rouen skipper carries the abbey's wine north and brings him books to look at (?)

lines.greet: A merchant. Good: you have seen other cities. Tell me, do they build their monks inside the wall or out?
lines.greet_again: You again. The walls at Holy Cross are up to my shoulder now. Come and see before you sell anything.
rumour: The count asked us all where to build. The old men said there were monks at the Holy Cross once. It was my family's land. I said so.
The abbey is to have the oratory at Soulac, with the pine wood and the fishery. Somebody must carry the fish. Why not a man with a boat?
The charter ends with a curse: the lot of Judas, and a hundred pounds of gold. Nobody here has seen one pound.
lines.saying: What old men remember is a charter nobody can burn.
lines.to_heir: Your father brought lead for our roof and would not be thanked. His name is in the book. Go and read it; I will show you where.
lines.farewell: God keep you on the water. If you pass Soulac, look at our dunes and tell me if the sand has moved.

people.source: Real: Trencard, a young noble 'learned in letters', who answered Count William that old men remembered monks at the oratory of the Holy Cross, on his family's land, and gave it up (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 2; dossier 3, 7). Nothing else is known of him: his dates, looks and later life are invented (?). The curse of Judas's lot and 100 pounds of gold is the charter's own.

people.name: Geoffrey
people.trait: A Frank from the north set over Gascons and Aquitanians: honest, orderly, and aware that every one of them can hear it in his speech.
people.want: His churches in stone and their rents in his own clerks' hands, and peace between the men who say they are counts.
people.fear: A year with two counts and no duke, when every armed man remembers what he is owed.
people.voice: Measured, in the northern way of speaking that the town finds stiff. Says 'it is written' and then shows you where. Does not joke; smiles when others do.
people.looks: About forty-five in 1030, tall, clean-shaven and tonsured, a plain dark cope with one band of gold thread, a staff with a curled ivory head, a ring over his glove.
knows: which churches hold which tolls: Saint-Macaire's road toll and its three measures of salt
what was sworn at Charroux and who has broken it
who the duke is this year, or who says he is
where a stranger may be buried and for what gift

ties.note: the old man knows where every charter lies; the archbishop asks him before he asks his clerks (?)
a Frank by birth, he still has letters from the north and wants more (?)
they have not met; the duke at Poitiers has had a painted book from the English king, and the archbishop would give much to see it (Adémar of Chabannes (?))

lines.greet: You are welcome in this church. You are from the north, as I am. Here that is forgiven on feast days.
lines.greet_again: The merchant who gives before he asks. Sit. I have a letter for the north and nobody I trust to carry it.
rumour: I was anointed at Blaye, before the duke and all his men. A bishop made in front of that many swords remembers it.
It was sworn at Charroux that nobody takes a poor man's ox, his ass or his pig. I read it out each year. Each year it is news.
Two men say they are count here. I pray for both by name at the same Mass. It saves time.
lines.saying: Build in stone. Fire has a long memory and wood a short one.
lines.to_heir: Your father is in our book of the dead, on the same leaf as a duke. I looked. Come and see it.
lines.farewell: Go in peace. Remember Saint Seurin on his day, wherever the wind has put you.

people.source: Real: Geoffrey II, 'a Frank by birth, honest in his ways', chosen and anointed at Blaye in 1027 before Duke Sancho's assembly, died 10 July 1043, buried at Saint Seurin (Gallia Christiana II cols 796-803; dossier 3). The Saint-Macaire toll and salt: Instrumenta no. 4; Charroux 989: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concile_de_Charroux; the contest for the county after 1039: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comté_de_Bordeaux. His birth year, looks and manner are invented.

people.name: Felix
people.trait: Sells the oil that comes up from the south by river and cart: a soft-spoken man with a long memory for debts and a longer one for who paid early.
people.want: The island monks' debt for last year's jars settled, by them or by anyone; a carrier for the jars who does not stack them under casks.
people.fear: A cracked jar, which is a debt nobody will own; a year when the south sends nothing.
people.voice: Quiet Romance, patient, names a sum and then the saint's day it falls due.
people.looks: About forty-five, plump, oiled grey hair, a long undyed linen tunic with stained cuffs, a dipping rod and a string of little tasting spoons at his belt.
knows: what a jar of oil costs this year and why
which churches burn oil and which only tallow, and who is behind in paying
the island of the three lamps: forty measures went there in the founder's day
which carters from the south can be trusted with jars

ties.note: Has sold the island its lamp oil for twenty years; is owed for last year's jars and has not stopped the next ones.
Her house bought oil of his father. She pays on the day and tells him what it used to cost.
The pilot tells him which hulls ride steady enough for jars.

lines.greet: Oil? It is dear. It is dear every year and this year I can say why. Taste first. Then tell me where you are bound.
lines.greet_again: The jars came whole? Then you may have six more, and I will not ask what you stood them on.
rumour: The monks of the salt island owe me for nine jars. They have burned three lamps since their founder died. I would not be the man who put one out.
A Frank asked me for oil to dress mail. I sold it. Oil does not ask what it is for.
lines.saying: Oil and truth come to the top. Oil is quicker.
lines.farewell: Stand them upright and wedge them with straw. If one cracks, bring me the pieces. I like to know.

people.source: invented (Felix, a common Roman and saint's name in Aquitaine (?)), to give the Herio cellarer's tie and the story herio.three_lamps their man. The Bordeaux oil ship and the forty measures are in the Life of Saint Philibert (Vita Filiberti c. 27 in Poupardin's numbering, as read in dossiers/herio.md). No oil seller of Bordeaux is named in any source.

stories.title: How the city fell: three tellings
stories.summary: From 844 the Northmen are on the Garonne, and for four years the city's wine has no way out but a small boat on a night ebb. In 848 the wall is passed in the dark, and afterwards every port tells a different story of who let them in.
stories.picture: Night on a wide river: a small boat low with casks slipping down on the ebb without a light, the black city wall behind her, and far downstream a line of red fires on the bank.

beats.text: A fleet goes by in the grey before dawn, upriver, rowing. Nobody on the wall shouts. By noon the town knows they are bound for Toulouse and that nobody will stand against them.
Men in from the Saintes road swear on the relics that Count Seguin was taken and killed and Saintes is burning. Natan says sworn news is worth silver in the north, if it gets there first.
A clerk who writes for an abbot upriver pays for the news from Aquitaine, sworn to. He says only: every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.

The Danes lie round the wall and have done for months. Casks are stacked to the roofs and nobody is buying. A boat that can get out on a night ebb and past the fires can have wine at a third of its price.
Natan asks for passage for nine people and a chest of scrolls to the Loire. He will pay in wine, in silver, or in a debt his sons will honour. Others at the gate watch who you take.
In Lent the king takes nine Danish ships on the Dordogne and the town rings its bells. Some weeks later the city is entered by night and burns. If you are in the river you see the glow from Blaye.

A salt man says Pippin's own men opened a gate, to spite King Charles. At Parisius a clerk says the Jews betrayed it. A survivor says the watch was drunk and a ladder is a ladder. You were there, or near.
Nine people of Bordeaux and a chest of scrolls live in a hired house by the port, if a boat was found for them. Their sons trade in salt and wine, and say what they saw to anyone who asks.
Einold writes the fall of Bordeaux into his list in three lines, one for each telling, and marks none of them true.

endings.how: You bought in the siege and ran the casks out on night ebbs.
endings.text: Three runs past the fires, and the wine sold at the Loire for four times what it cost. The sellers inside the wall ate that winter because of it, and say so.
endings.reward: Wine at a third of its price in 847; a very large profit; standing with the townsfolk of Burdigala that an heir inherits; the unlock burdigala.night_ebb.

endings.how: You gave your hold to Natan's household and the scrolls and took them to the Loire.
endings.text: Nine people and a chest ashore at Namnetis, and little cargo to show for the voyage. Natan's sons trade from the Loire for two generations and do not forget whose boat it was.
endings.reward: A debt honoured in full by his sons (a large sum, paid later); a factor's welcome at Namnetis; the unlock burdigala.natans_word; when the tellings are told, you may say what you saw and be believed.

endings.how: You traded with the fleet on the river: bread and wine for silver by weight.
endings.text: The Danes pay well and at once. The town learns of it before the tide turns. After the fire a survivor names you among those who fed them.
endings.reward: Good silver now; the Northmen on the western rivers know your sail and may let it pass; shunned at Burdigala for a generation, and the bishop's door shut.

endings.how: You heard the news in 844 and did not come back up the river until it was over.
endings.text: You lost nothing. The house by the Broken Tower is a burned gable, and nobody at the gate knows your face.
endings.reward: Nothing lost and nothing gained: the people who knew you here are gone, and standing in the town starts again from nothing.

stories.reward: The dearest cheap wine on the chart for those who dare it, a family that owes you its lives, or a name with the fleets: and a say in which telling the ports believe.

stories.title: The weight of a Bordeaux penny
stories.summary: From 814 the city strikes the king's penny in good silver from Melle. Melle burns in 848, and when coin comes back it is the counts' own, as light as half a penny, and worth exactly what a scale says.
stories.picture: A moneyer's scale with a fat old penny in one pan and two thin ones in the other, not quite balancing; behind, a board with bad coins nailed to it.

beats.text: Bertric strikes pennies with the city's name in two lines. He shows you the right weight on his beam and lets you feel a good one and a short one with your eyes shut.
A new die: the city's name round a little temple with four columns. Bertric says the temple is no building he knows, and the silver from Melle comes later every year.
A salt skipper from the Bay heard it a fortnight ago: Melle is burned, where the king's silver is dug. Good pennies will be worth keeping.
The duke's pennies say SANCHIVS round a worn mark that was once a king's name. Some weigh half of others. The moneyer shrugs: they pass here by tale, and nowhere else.
A changer in the north turns a Bordeaux penny over, laughs, and puts it on the scale. Sold by weight it is fair silver; offered at face it is an insult.
One of the king's ten mints gives a penny and a half of the new coin for a fat old penny of Bordeaux. The moneyer asks where there are more.

endings.how: You learned the beam from Bertric, or carried your own scale, and took the thin pennies only by weight.
endings.text: You buy wine with good pennies counted and take change weighed. The moneyer thinks you rude and the wine sellers think you clever.
endings.reward: No loss on Bordeaux coin in any era; a small steady gain carrying thin pennies north as silver; the thread's flag sv_scale counts here as it does in the north.

endings.how: You kept back the good pennies of Louis and Lothar when Melle burned.
endings.text: Twenty years on, a fat old penny with the city's name buys what two new ones do. Your heir finds the bag and understands what you were doing.
endings.reward: A purse that grows by sitting: old Bordeaux pennies are worth half as much again after 848 at any mint that still strikes (Quentovic, Rotomagus).

endings.how: You carried the duke's thin pennies north and tried to pass them by tale.
endings.text: The first changer weighs them. The second calls the reeve. You pay the difference and a little more, and the story travels.
endings.reward: Nothing gained: a fine, and the changers of the Channel ports cool for a year. Bertric's successor finds it very funny.

stories.reward: Knowing what this city's coin is worth in each age, which is money in itself; and a moneyer who lets you use his beam.

stories.title: The poet of the city
stories.summary: Placidina keeps one old book: the verses a man of this city wrote about it when Rome still ruled, and about every other famous city too. The abbot at Tours wants a copy, the city has a clerk who can make one, and in 848 everything in the city that can burn will.
stories.picture: An old woman in a dark veil reading aloud from a worn book by a hearth in a room built against a Roman wall, a river pilot and a merchant listening, a vine at the door.

beats.text: On a slow evening Placidina reads to the room from the old book, and puts it into plain speech after: walls four-square, towers in the clouds, a whole sea gliding up the river with its fleets. It is still true, less the fleets.
A monk bound up the Loire for Tours says his abbot collects what the old poets wrote and has heard of a book at Bordeaux. He would pay for a true copy, and pay better than for wine.
One clerk of Saint Andrew's can copy a fair hand. He wants skins, ink and forty days, and Placidina wants to know who the copy is for before the book leaves her house.
She left the book to the bishop's church. It lies in the chained cupboard. A clerk will lend it against a pledge, for copying; in the siege year he would give it to anyone who could carry it out.
The cupboard is ash. If a copy went up the Loire, it is the only one that speaks of this city in her own man's voice. If you kept one in the chest, clerks ask to see it.
The schoolmaster at Saint-Wandrille has two lines of the Bordeaux poet in a grammar book, quoted for a rare word (?). He did not know there was more.

endings.how: You paid for the copy and carried it dry to the Loire for Tours.
endings.text: The abbot's scribes copy it again in their clear new hand. Placidina hears that her city's poet is read at Saint Martin's, and pours you the good cask.
endings.reward: A fine payment from Tours; the thread's flag bk_carried; Placidina a fast friend, and the unlock burdigala.placidinas_cellar.

endings.how: You took the old book itself out of the city in the siege, on a pledge or on trust.
endings.text: The book outlives the church that owned it. When an archbishop sits in Bordeaux again, the house can give it back, or name its price.
endings.reward: The book in the hold (goods: books), worth more than the boat; given back after 887, it makes the church here the house's friend for good and counts as the work 'a book for a church'.

endings.how: You had a second copy made for yourself and kept it.
endings.text: Beornwine reads it aloud on calm days, slowly and truly. The crew learn the names of twenty cities none of them will see.
endings.reward: A text for the chest (the Order of Famous Cities, the lines on Bordeaux); morale on long passages; the thread's flag bk_knows_worth.

endings.how: You did nothing, or the copy was spoiled by water.
endings.text: The book burns with the cupboard in 848. Old people can say a few lines of it. Then nobody can.
endings.reward: Nothing; if a copy was lost in your care, the thread's flag bk_lost, and clerks along the Loire hear of it.

stories.reward: A book carried is worth more than a hold of wine, and here it buys the widow's friendship as well: the one person in the city who knows everybody's business since Rome.

stories.title: The crown that waits at Bordeaux
stories.summary: In 906 a king in Spain agrees to buy a crown of gold and gems from the clergy of Tours, to be left with Count Amalvinus until his ships come in May. Somebody has to bring a crown down the Loire and through the Northmen's sea, and the count would rather it were not his own men.
stories.picture: A count in a blue cloak lifting a cloth from a jewelled gold crown on a table in a bare hall, a merchant beside him, and through the door the masts of two strange ships on the river.

beats.text: Amalvinus unfolds a letter and has it read: the king of Spain, 'our friend', a crown, the clergy of Saint Martin, ships in May. He asks whether your boat is fast, and whether you are.
Two canons of Tours wait at the Loire with a small heavy chest and four frightened servants. They want a receipt cut on a tally, a count of the stones, and an oath.
Sails off the island, lying still. A man who carries nothing would run in under the land and wait a day. A man who carries a crown has to decide what he looks like.
The count counts the stones himself, twice, against the tally. Then he locks the chest in the chapel and you both wait for May.

beats.when: year >= 906 and year < 908 and month >= 5 and month < 8
beats.text: Either two ships with strange high stems come up on the flood, with men whose Romance nobody here can quite follow, or the pilot's grandson shakes his head each morning.
Count Robert is lay abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours as well as of Saint Denis's (?). His steward asks what boat the canons found for their chest, and writes the name down.
The Northmen on the Seine have heard that something small and heavy is going down the Loire to the sea. A man of Rollo's asks about it as a man asks about the weather.

endings.how: You brought the chest whole and the ships came.
endings.text: The king's shipmen pay the canons' price in gold coin of a kind you have not seen, and Amalvinus pays you in silver and in wine. The Spanish master asks what else the north sells.
endings.reward: 600 d from the count and a tun of his best wine; the canons of Tours owe the house a favour on the Loire; the unlock burdigala.spanish_ships (oil, wax and pepper to be had at Burdigala in May).

endings.how: You brought the chest whole and no ship came, that May or the next.
endings.text: The crown stays in the count's chapel. He pays you for the carriage and says the king is a busy man. In later years some say there never was a letter.
endings.reward: 300 d for the carriage; Amalvinus a friend; a story that buys a cup in any hall from the Loire to the Seine, and a doubt you can sell to the canons of Tours.

endings.how: The chest went to the Northmen off the island, or to the sea, or a stone was missing at the count.
endings.text: The tally is laid beside what is left. The canons write to every church on the Loire. The count is courteous and does not ask you in again.
endings.reward: Nothing; a debt to Saint Martin's that follows the house, and the Loire's churches cool until it is paid. If you bought your passage from the Northmen with it, they remember that too.

stories.reward: One voyage with the dearest small cargo on the western sea: silver, the count's friendship, and perhaps the first ships from Spain.

stories.title: What the old men remember
stories.summary: About 975 Count William asks his household where to build a monastery, inside the city or out, and young Trencard answers with what old men remember: monks in the marsh, on his family's land. A house begun again needs lead, timber, fish and friends, and the charter ends with a curse on whoever takes any of it back.
stories.picture: A half-built stone church on a rise in a reed marsh, scaffolding of poles, a slight young man in green pointing with a rolled parchment, monks carrying a beam along a log causeway.

beats.text: The count puts the question to the whole hall. Trencard says what the old men told him and gives up the land where he stands. Afterwards he asks you what a roof of lead costs in the north.
Abbot Elis has thirteen monks, walls to the shoulder and no roof. He needs lead, oak and a bell, and can pay in wine not yet grown and prayers already begun.
The abbey's fishery at Soulac, at the river mouth, wants a boat to bring its catch up in Lent and take salt down. The monks ask a man they know before a man they do not.
The archbishop is back from Charroux with what the bishops swore: a curse on any who break a church, strike an unarmed clerk or take a poor man's beast. He wants it carried and read at the Loire.
The canons of Saint Seurin keep a list of those who may lie among the stone coffins. A gift to their church puts a name on it. A broken gift, their charter says, is the burial of asses.
Thorold has three casks of Holy Cross wine under the wall, and a book wrapped in his cloak for an old man in Bordeaux who can read it.
What the bishops swore at Charroux is read out at the Loire: a curse on whoever breaks a church, strikes an unarmed clerk or takes a poor man's beast. The count's men stand at the back.

endings.how: You brought lead or oak for the roof and took the abbey's wine in years to come.
endings.text: The church is roofed before the second winter. Your name is on a leaf of the abbey's book, and three casks wait in the press-house each Martinmas.
endings.reward: The work burdigala.work.holy_cross at a third less; aquitaine_wine at the abbey's own price each year; Trencard and the abbot fast friends; burial among the monks.

endings.how: You took the Soulac run: fish up in Lent, salt down.
endings.text: A dull, sure trade that pays every spring. The monks' serfs at Soulac know your sail, and the pilot's kin show you the mouth for nothing.
endings.reward: A standing commission each Lent (dried_fish up, sea_salt down); act:hire_pilot free at Burdigala; the unlock burdigala.soulac_run.

endings.how: You promised the abbey and did not deliver, or sold their lead elsewhere.
endings.text: The monks read the curse at the end of their charter aloud at the gate, with your name where the breaker's goes. In a town this size everybody hears.
endings.reward: Nothing gained: no burial at Saint Seurin, cool with every church in Aquitaine until amends are made (twice the gift).

stories.reward: A share in the one thing in this city that is growing: wine at the abbey's price, a place among the dead, and friends who can write.

works.name: A share of vines on the gravel
works.what: A few rows on the dry gravel west of the wall, worked on halves by a family that has always worked them, with a place in a press-house at the vintage. Bought from a widow, a count's steward or, after 977, leased from Holy Cross for a life.
works.needs: A host in the city (standing 30 here, or Placidina's friendship, or the abbey's after 977); a seller.
works.gives: Each year at Martinmas three casks of new wine (aquitaine_wine) wait in the press-house: none in a frost year or a siege year, five in a great one. Unfetched wine is sold there at the cheap price.
works.picture: Low vines on pale stony ground in October light, a woman cutting grapes into a basket, the city wall and the white pillars behind.
works.source: works_793.json vineyard_share (the shared work, its cost and yield); 'lands with vines' given to Holy Cross before 977 (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 2). For 793 the vineyard rests on the city's Roman fame alone: 'documents are lacking' (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vignoble_de_Bordeaux) (?).

works.name: A store under the wall
works.what: A dry stone room in the foot of a wall tower by the water gate, with a new door and a bar: Roman work with nobody's name on it, to be had from whoever holds the city for a rent and a gift.
works.needs: The count's leave (act:audience at the hall), and no siege that year.
works.gives: Up to thirty units wait here (act:store); wine and salt keep twice as long under stone. What lies here when the city is taken in 848 is lost unless it was carried out.
works.picture: The foot of a round stone tower with a new oak door let into an old arch, casks being rolled in, the river beyond.
works.source: works_793.json storehouse (the shared work and its cost); the wall with towers about every 50 m: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remparts_et_portes_de_ville_de_Bordeaux. Letting a tower as a store is the game's (?).

works.name: Your stretch of the wall
works.what: After the fire the city mends its Roman wall with blocks sledged from the Arenas, and each household of standing takes a stretch to rebuild and to man. A stranger with silver may take one and be a stranger no longer.
works.needs: A store or a share of vines here; the count's leave (act:fund_work at the hall).
works.gives: What a raid takes from the house's works and stores in this port is halved, and a small raid takes nothing. Standing rises with the count and the townsfolk; the house is named among the men of the city.
works.picture: Men on a wooden scaffold setting a squared block into a gap in a high grey wall, oxen and a sledge below, the broken arches of the Arenas far behind.
works.source: works_793.json wall_share (the shared work and its cost); the wall strengthened in the late 9th century, when armed men first appear (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histoire_de_Bordeaux); the amphitheatre as a quarry (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Gallien). Shares by household are the game's (?).

works.name: A roof for Holy Cross
works.what: Count William is rebuilding the monastery in the marsh for thirteen monks. The walls are his; the roof, the lead and the bell are for whoever will give them and have a name in the abbey's book for it.
works.needs: Abbot Elis's or Trencard's good word (act:fund_work at Holy Cross). Lead or oak_timber brought by the house takes a third off.
works.gives: Standing with the Christians of the port and its region rises greatly; the abbot is a friend to the heir too; the house may lodge and be buried at the abbey; its wine is sold to the house at the abbey's own price.
works.picture: Monks and laymen hauling a sheet of grey lead up to the roof timbers of a new stone church standing in reeds, a bell waiting on the ground on a sledge.
works.source: works_793.json church_rebuilt (the shared work and its cost); Holy Cross 'destroyed by the pagans' and rebuilt before 977 by William the Good for thirteen monks and Abbot Elis (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 2; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbatiale_Sainte-Croix_de_Bordeaux). The lead roof is assumed (?).

works.name: A stone coffin by Saint Seurin
works.what: A place in the field of the dead outside the gate of Jove, near the saint: an old stone coffin emptied and washed, a lid, and a name in the church's list. Everybody who can afford to wait for the Judgment here does.
works.needs: A gift to the church and a clean name: nobody under a charter's curse lies here.
works.gives: The house's dead may be buried here (act:bury) and remembered each year (act:remember): the heir begins with the standing of a family of the city, and the canons (from about 990) pray for the house by name.
works.picture: Rows of grey stone coffins in long grass outside a low old church, one lid stood open against its box, an old woman with candles, larks overhead.
works.source: The grave field at Saint Seurin, 4th to 13th century: 435 burials dug, 265 in stone coffins stacked up to five deep (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nécropole_Saint-Seurin_de_Bordeaux); the curse that a breaker 'shall never be buried in the cemetery' (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 3). Reusing a coffin is what the stacking suggests; the price is this file's (?).

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The river's own small boat: fishermen and ferrymen work the bend and the marsh streams in them, and the boat bank can build one from Garonne oak before Lent.
ships.picture: A small open boat on river gravel with two men fitting a thwart, the city wall and its towers behind.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json (west_small_boat: frankish, estuaries and creeks); no yard is recorded at Bordeaux (dossier 3) (?)

ships.note: Flat barges bring wine, grain and timber down the Garonne on the current and are hauled or sold at the town. An old one is cheap; she will not live outside the river mouth.
ships.picture: A long flat barge heaped with casks drifting down a wide brown river on the ebb, a man at a sweep, vines on a low hill beyond.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json (river_barge); the Garonne navigable to Toulouse, where a fleet went in 844 (Annales Bertiniani). Barges on the Garonne in these years are assumed (?).

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The right boat for this river mouth: small enough for the banks, able to cross to the Loire in fair weather. After 977 Holy Cross keeps one for its fishery at Soulac and orders another when the house offers to pay half.
ships.picture: A ten-pace sailing boat with a square sail and six oars coming in past a low point of dunes and pines, baskets of fish amidships, a monk in the stern.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json (coaster_minster_ship: the ships of the toll charters); Soulac's oratory, pine wood and fishery given to Holy Cross before 977 (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta nos 2, 4). The abbey's boat is assumed (?).

ships.note: Sea-going hulls come here seldom, for wine, from the Loire and Armorica; one that has touched the banks is sometimes sold where she lies by a master who has had enough of the river.
ships.picture: A broad merchant ship lying over on a sandbank at low water in a huge flat estuary, her crew carrying casks ashore across the wet sand.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json (north_sea_merchant_ship: frankish, Neustria); sea ties with Spain and Armorica are of the 6th and 7th centuries (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_de_Bordeaux): for 793 the sea trade is assumed (?).

ships.note: In the years when fleets winter in the country, a Northman with too many ships and too few men will sell one for silver by weight, to anybody, at the river bank. The town watches who buys.
ships.picture: A lean clinker ship with a high curved stem drawn up on a river bank in winter mist, shields off her rail, two Northmen and a cloaked merchant weighing silver on a small scale.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json (norse_allround_ship); Northmen wintering in the country in 848, 855 and 864 (Boutoulle 2008) and Asgeir's fleet sailing from and to Bordeaux in 851-852 (Chronicon Fontanellense). Whether they held the town is disputed, and the sale is the game's (?).

sayings.text: Her goodly walls four-square raise lofty towers so high that their tops pierce the soaring clouds.
sayings.source: Ausonius, Order of Famous Cities XX, tr. H. G. Evelyn-White (1919): of Bordeaux; said here by Placidina

sayings.text: The tide brings a whole sea gliding onward with its fleets.
sayings.source: Ausonius, Order of Famous Cities XX, tr. H. G. Evelyn-White (1919), shortened: the river at Bordeaux

sayings.text: Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.
sayings.source: Luke 11:17, as Lupus of Ferrières quotes it on the news of Seguin's death in 845 (letter 31); the dossier's rendering

sayings.text: He shall never be buried in the cemetery, but laid in the burial of asses.
sayings.source: A charter of the canons of Saint Seurin, about 990 (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 3), after Jeremiah 22:19; our rendering

sayings.text: Let him have the lot of Judas, and pay a hundred pounds of gold and a thousand of silver. (Said of any bill nobody means to pay.)
sayings.source: The curse of William the Good's charter for Holy Cross (Gallia Christiana II, Instrumenta no. 2); the joke on it is invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Never call an Aquitanian a Frank. He will forgive you, and remember.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the rule is Design/content/peoples/frankish.md

sayings.text: The Franks say we shave our necks and wear our clothes short. We say a Frank has never been warm.
sayings.source: invented, turning the northern monk's mockery of Aquitanian dress about 1000 (Rodulfus Glaber III.40 (?)); for use after 990

sayings.text: The sea lends the river to us twice a day and takes it back.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the tide runs far above the town (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gironde_(estuaire))

sayings.text: A wide river and an open river are two rivers.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the estuary is up to 12 km wide and full of banks

sayings.text: When men swear to news, it is bad and it is true.
sayings.source: invented, from Lupus's remark that men came from Aquitaine affirming Seguin's death 'even on oath' (letter 31)

easter_eggs.text: Count the pillars from the river: twenty-four, with a carved figure over each. Eight hundred years after you, seventeen still stand; then a king has them pulled down to clear the ground before a fortress.
easter_eggs.source: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piliers_de_Tutelle: 24 columns when whole, 17 standing in 1669, demolished under Louis XIV (the reason from memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: Among the stone coffins at Saint Seurin a gravedigger turns up a big clay wine jar with a baby's bones in it, and puts it back without a word. There are dozens. The city buried its infants in what its wine came in.
Bertric's new die of the 840s shows a temple with columns. He says it is no building he knows. Walk out of the north gate and look up.
easter_eggs.source: Lothar I's penny BVRDICALA round a temple, 1.60 g (Prou 1896). The temple is the common Carolingian type, not a portrait of the pillars: the likeness is the player's to enjoy (?)

easter_eggs.text: The west gate is still called Jove's. Ask anyone who Jove was and they will say a saint, or a count, or the man who built the gate.
easter_eggs.source: Porta Jovia, the west gate (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remparts_et_portes_de_ville_de_Bordeaux); the old gods are only ruins and a gate's name (dossier 6)

easter_eggs.text: The keeper at Holy Cross shows a slab where an abbot from the Loire lies who died here on a journey, a hundred years before you. He has the name nearly right.
easter_eggs.source: Mommolin, abbot of Fleury, died at Holy Cross about 679 (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbatiale_Sainte-Croix_de_Bordeaux)

easter_eggs.text: There is nothing on the altar at Saint Seurin but a cloth and a lamp. A generation after the game ends, a song will lay a great ivory horn there, 'where pilgrims see it'.
easter_eggs.source: The Song of Roland, of about 1100 (?), lays Roland's horn on Saint Seurin's altar (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilique_Saint-Seurin_de_Bordeaux); not to be shown in these years (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: Placidina's poet praised a little spring in the middle of the city as a goddess, by name. Nobody alive can point to it. She thinks it is under the count's stable.
easter_eggs.source: Ausonius, Order of Famous Cities XX, on the fountain Divona (Evelyn-White 1919; from memory, not in the dossier (?)); the stable is invented

unlocks.what: Amantius's marks for the river mouth
unlocks.how: Take him as pilot three times and pay him at the gate before you sell, each time.
unlocks.gives: The house knows the channel: no pilot is needed between the sea and Burdigala, and grounding on the banks becomes doubtful instead of likely. His grandson keeps the marks true for the heir.

unlocks.what: Wine from the widow's own cellar
unlocks.how: Be her friend: bring news from the Loire, a clerk who can read, or carry the copy of her book (the story burdigala.poets_book).
unlocks.gives: act:buy_at_source at the house by the Broken Tower: aquitaine_wine at the made price all year, tasted from the middle of the cask. Lodging there costs nothing.

unlocks.what: The count's leave to trade across the river
unlocks.how: A gift and an audience at the hall, and no mail or blades sold to the Gascons.
unlocks.gives: The Gascons' bank is open to the house: horses and cattle_hides to be had there at source (?), and the toll at the water gate is waived. Lost, with a fine, if arms are found going across.

unlocks.what: The use of the moneyer's beam
unlocks.how: Bring Bertric foreign silver twice and accept his weighing without argument (814 to 847); afterwards, a gift to his successor.
unlocks.gives: act:test_silver and act:change_coin here cost nothing, and the loss on old or foreign coin at this mint is halved.

unlocks.how: Run the river in the siege year (the story burdigala.three_tellings, ending ran_the_wine).
unlocks.gives: The house may leave Burdigala by night without a pilot, and a chase begun in the river mouth is one word less likely to catch her.

unlocks.how: Carry his household out before the city falls (the story burdigala.three_tellings, ending carried_them_out).
unlocks.gives: A factor's welcome at Namnetis for two generations: goods left with his sons are sold in the dear season for a twentieth, and they lend to the house without a pledge.

unlocks.how: Bring the crown to Count Amalvinus whole (the story burdigala.kings_crown, ending crown_delivered).
unlocks.gives: From 906, in May and June, olive_oil, wax and pepper are in the market at Burdigala when the Spanish ships are in (?), and their master buys frisian_cloth and swords at a good price.

unlocks.how: Take the abbey's fish boat (the story burdigala.old_mens_memory, ending the_fish_boat).
unlocks.gives: A commission every Lent from 977: dried_fish from the river mouth to the city and sea_salt back, a small sure profit, and a safe beach at the river mouth to wait for a tide.
